title: Some lessons from nearly a year of building in Godot with Claude
author: puddhoggstudios
selftext:
Hey crew. I’m about to publish my first game, Crestbound, on Steam in a few weeks. I’ve been working on it in an AI workflow for about a year (started as a new years resolution) and have learned a ton in that time that I’d like to share. 

I’ve checked out this sub a lot for ways to improve my workflow, and for solutions to problems I hadn’t discovered yet. Hopefully this post can likewise help some others starting out.

https://i.redd.it/9too51ls78zh1.png

**The Game**

Crestbound is a turn-based tactical RPG slash mercenary-company management sim. The game I’ve always wanted to play is a hybrid of Final Fantasy Tactics and Football Manager, so that’s what I set out to make. You scout and sign units to multi-year contracts, manage weekly payroll and injuries in a worker-placement camp, and fight on a 16x11 hex grid with a pip-based action economy and pace timeline.

https://i.redd.it/enhqy47i88zh1.png

The scope is too big, because of course it is, and it would probably take years without AI workflows. Gemini told me after reading the GDD that the scope represents “a life’s work”, which is a bit of an exaggeration. 

What I’m releasing this month is the first of four continents in-game: this slice has 10 Crests to discover and research across 5 regions. Each region has distinct enemies and battlegrounds, with collectible fragments of 2 of the Crests.   
  
Each Crest has 50 nodes. Crest research nodes unlock weapons, abilities, passives and equipment upgrades. 

https://i.redd.it/3k5lga2y78zh1.png

At the highest rank, units can slot 4 abilities and 4 passives, plus those that are on their weapons, so there are already countless ways to build out units. Of course that only matters if you can keep them on the payroll, and they don’t suffer a catastrophic ACL tear.

https://i.redd.it/cpkh9axd88zh1.png

**How It’s Made**

The game is made in Godot. It is in a 100% data-first architecture, with zero hard-coded content IDs. This was really important to me from the beginning, which helped the content scale very easily. This meant that I front-loaded a lot of time in the beginning making the schema and the action resolver, even for a simple Slash, before I got to see the payoff.

But now adding a new ability on existing seams takes 30 seconds – even if it seems fairly complex. For example, if I wanted to add a Sticky Bomb ability right now, which targets an enemy unit within 4 hexes, applies a Sticky Bomb status, transforms the Sticky Bomb ability into Detonate, and makes Detonate explode the Sticky Bomb for a fire damage blast in an area around the target, it would take no longer than it did to write out that paragraph. All the engine seams exist, and each of those steps are just parts of the JSON. 

I love this, because I am a diseased person who wants to add every combination of abilities I’ve ever enjoyed in any game.   
  
**Workflow**

I spent a long time on a GDD. This is mostly because I didn’t think actually making a game was possible on my own, so making the GDD was a creative outlet. This turned out to be quite helpful for the model later on.

When I started out I was using ChatGPT to code, because that was the one I’d heard of. I wasn’t even using the terminal, just literally copy and pasting code from the chatbot like an idiot. 

Once I started using Claude Code and Codex, things obviously took off. I prefer Claude Code mainly because it seems to understand and respect the codebase better. I run an /engine-review skill that checks every commit to ensure that no hard-coded content ID or duplicated seam was added, and Claude rarely fails that compared to Codex.  
  
I DO use Codex for the visual assets. This is especially great now that imagegen is right in Codex. Typically I will use Claude Code to generate the kits in Blender, and then generate guide images and prompts in a handoff folder that is given to Codex. 

The biggest problem I had over the past 6 months was changes to ChatGPT models removing the ability to replicate the style I already had in-game several times. Each model would be able to replicate the style, color palette, paint and proportions fairly well, but once an upgrade came to the imagegen model it was very difficult to get it back. 

This mainly burned me because my asset scope is also out of control. I wanted every region to have it’s own set of 10 faces for units, so that units scouted from that area were distinct. Each face has 5 expression sprites though, so keeping hundreds of faces consistent was a headache. 

Anyway, happy to answer any questions about the process. It has been a dream of mine to make a game since I first played FF7, I can't believe that it’s become possible.

comments.author: Esayemuss
comments.body: Thanks for sharing! Could you go a little more into your asset generation pipeline? What is the kit in blender?? I assume the grey boxed assets to correct specs?

replies.author: puddhoggstudios
replies.body:
Yes for sure.

The game is 2.5D wth a fixed camera at a 30° angle. iWe (me and Claude) don't use an off-the shelf kit for it, it's a set of Python scripts that build the geometry in Blender 5.2, mostly headlessly. 

Each location has a small kit of shapes like rocks, trees, and other objects. Scripts build those for the game board, then it's rendered in Blender in a toon-shaped guide, then painted in Codex with a handoff guide that Claude writes.

For obstacles, the painting is fitted back onto the model and projected on from the camera angle, then exported as a GLB that Godot loads. Ground plates start from a guide drawn from the real board layout, so the painted ground lines up with the hexes.

It started out completely 2D, with single flat images for the battlefield. Migrating to 2.5D with light and the fixed camera angle took about a week, with 3 sessions updating battlegrounds concurrently.

replies.author: puddhoggstudios
replies.body:
Also, the biggest win I had as far as asset generation when I stopped trying to use ChatGPT / Codex for the assets myself, and instead got Claude to write the handoffs for Codex in a queue MD. Everything started getting way more consistent and way faster after that.

The queue md file also instructs Codex where to export the assets to and where to pause. Claude picks up again once the assets are in the folder, implements them, then adds different reference files to the folder that Codex uses for the next part of the queue. 

The only part that isn't automated yet is telling Codex to start again.

comments.author: Kooker321
comments.body:
Looks really promising! Can you share an option for people to playtest or check out your game when it's in beta? I'm also working on a turn based rpg (more akin to classic final fantasy and octopath traveler).

I'm using Claude Code and am getting great results, but I've heard good things about Codex, specifically for graphics/creating assets, which is Claude Code's weak spot. So far I've solved this successfully with Pixel Lab. But how do you migrate builds or instructions from one of these platforms to the other? Is it seamless? How does Codex's art compare? Does it utilize AI plug ins from other apps?

replies.author: puddhoggstudios
replies.body:
For this style of game, Codex has worked great for me. I haven't tried Pixel Lab but if I had seen it back when the game had a similar art style I may have gone pretty deep there. 

If you mean migrating between Claude Code and Codex, I don't have to migrate anything. Both have access to the repo, which has a folder of md files, one fact per file. The master memory.md has one line per memory. 

Both Claude and Codex can access that, so it's easy to jump back and forth. Both have total context of what's being worked on.

replies.author: Kooker321
replies.body: Yes, that's what I meant. What exactly do you mean by both have access to the repo?

replies.author: puddhoggstudios
replies.body:
I’ve connected both Claude Code and Codex to the GitHub repo, so when I start a session in either one they’re working on on branches from the same files. 

So the files, even the handoffs between them, are in that repo and I’m not manually giving any instructions back and forth to catch them up.

replies.author: Kooker321
replies.body: Ahh that makes sense! Thanks for explaining

replies.author: puddhoggstudios
replies.body: No prob! I'd never done any kind of coding before this, so it took months of manual back and forth before I realized the best practices.

comments.author: bootsfirst
comments.body: I’m curious about the Engine Review skill - how do you prompt it?

replies.author: puddhoggstudios
replies.body:
It’s a custom claude skill built to check for anything in new code that goes against the data first methodology I want. 

I asked Claude to describe it:

/engine-review is a custom Claude Code skill that audits a code change for anything that fights our data-driven architecture, like code that checks for one specific enemy by name, or balance numbers buried in logic. It compares the change against a written map of where each kind of thing belongs, and only calls a problem confirmed if it has verified that the better home already exists. Ideas that would need new engine work are marked as speculative. By default it only reports, and with --fix it applies just the confirmed findings without changing any balance values, then re-runs our checks.
